triage.summary: The corpus's account of differential press coverage operates on three distinct axes (geographic before 1905, publisher-based after 1905, retroactive erasure in terminal cases) rather than a single principle, and this structural variation should be made explicit in how the information lane is organized and tested.
triage.note: Critical gap: Ida B. Wells is absent despite being the central methodological and historical figure in differential lynching coverage (Southern Horrors, A Red Record, Free Speech destruction). Her work is both an ancestor of the corpus's own method and the best-documented instance of the phenomenon being described. Two testable mechanisms not tracked: (1) AP Southern member papers supplied Southern copy, collapsing the distinction between 'wire' and 'local white press'; (2) Tuskegee Institute and NAACP competing annual tallies from 1890s onward provide the standard quantitative base for testing differential reporting claims. Multiple entries in this lane are tier C with unsourced content flags (Thibodaux 2 of 6 unsourced, Ocoee 1 of 3), and Sand Creek and McKinley entries demonstrably failed corpus's own coverage tests, suggesting untested coverage claims should be flagged as hypotheses rather than findings.

trigger_context: Where does the legal authority for European colonization actually come from? Start at the beginning.
raw_content:
The corpus threads this as T-DISCOVERY-DOCTRINE, and it is one of the best-evidenced chains it holds — tier A almost the whole way, with the instruments naming each other in sequence rather than being assembled by inference.

The beginning is not 1492. It is the conversion of spiritual authority into legal warrant, which the corpus locates at Clermont in 1095: Urban II's preaching turns a religious claim into a title-producing instrument, and the entry states the Dum Diversas template is "present here in embryo — the Church declares a war just; the just war then produces legal title over conquered land" [E-W0-016-02]. The step that matters is the one after it. In 1209 Innocent III turns the same instrument on Latin Christians in Languedoc, which the corpus reads as the domestic proof that the tool works on anyone the Pope designates — "the domestic stress test before Dum Diversas exports the model globally" [E-W0-018-04].

Then the operative text, and it is worth being precise about what it says. Nicholas V's Dum Diversas of 18 June 1452 grants Alfonso V free faculty to invade, subdue and reduce to perpetual servitude "Saracens, pagans, and any other unbelievers and enemies of Christ wheresoever placed" — and the corpus's key observation is that the category is defined by jurisdiction to Christendom, not by race or geography [E-W1-001-01]. Romanus Pontifex in 1455 expands it into a full colonial charter with exclusive rights south of Cape Bojador [E-W1-003-02], and Calixtus III reaffirms both in 1456, which the corpus flags as the real structural point: papal bulls are institutional software that survives the individual pope's death and gets reconfirmed across successions [E-W1-004-02].

From there it partitions rather than expands. Alcáçovas in 1479 divides Atlantic maritime space between Castile and Portugal before Columbus sails [E-W1-006-01]. Inter Caetera in 1493 is the specific bull the corpus calls the kernel, granting Spain everything 100 leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde "not already occupied by any Christian prince" [E-W1-010-01]. Tordesillas moves the line to 370 leagues in 1494 [E-W1-011-01]. Cabot's 1496 patent is the English wedge, authorising claim to lands "which before this time were unknown to all Christians" [E-W1-012-02] — same qualifying phrase, different crown.

Two things about how the machinery actually ran. The title frequently preceded the contact: the Capitulations of Santa Fe of 17 April 1492 granted Columbus admiral, viceroy and governor titles over any lands discovered, heritable in perpetuity, before any land was reached — and the corpus marks its own reading of that as discovery-as-title-laundering, tier C inference rather than quoted text [E-W1-009-02]. And the consent was manufactured: the Requerimiento of 1513, read aloud in Spanish to Spanish-illiterate populations before attack, with non-response constituting casus belli [E-W1-015-02].

The transposition into ordinary commercial law happens in 1606. The Virginia Charter carries the non-Christian subjugation logic out of papal instrument and into English corporate drafting, where it "operates as ordinary commercial drafting," and the colonists hold land in free and common socage from the Manor at East-Greenwich — tenants, never owners [E-W2-002-02], [E-W2-002-01]. That is the corpus's nemo dat point: tenants cannot grant allodial title downstream.

The chain terminates in American federal law in 1823, when Marshall in Johnson v. McIntosh imports the papal-bull authority directly, reducing indigenous title to a "right of occupancy" and creating a federal monopsony on purchase [E-W4-027-02].

Now the part I would not let you walk past, because the corpus threads it deliberately. There is a documented sovereign admission running against the whole structure. In 1750 Britain — the sovereign from which the United States inherits its Discovery-Doctrine authority — signed a treaty acknowledging the Emperor of Morocco's sovereignty over "all the West of Africa," 73 years before Johnson v. McIntosh [w3-1750-legal]. Morocco then demonstrated the capacity that period international law required of a sovereignty claim: repelling the French at Larache in 1765 [w3-1765-military] and expelling Portugal from Mazagan in 1769 after a 267-year occupation, closing an enclave held under the earliest Discovery-Doctrine bulls [w3-1769-military]. And the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with Morocco was ratified 18 July 1787, eleven months before the Constitution entered force, so it attaches to federal law the instant federal law exists [w3-1787-legal], [w3-1787-certification].

The issuer itself has since repudiated the instruments. On 30 March 2023 the Vatican formally repudiated Dum Diversas, Romanus Pontifex and Inter Caetera — and the corpus is careful here in a way worth respecting: the repudiation is the record; that present-day title chains descend from these bulls is the corpus's inference, and the statement makes no claim about any present-day government [E-W6-027-01].

One vocabulary note. "Software," "Hardware," the "Noun and the Adjective," "allodial title" as used above — those are this audit's analytical frame, not terms from the scholarship on the Doctrine of Discovery. The instruments and dates are standard; the framing that reads them as one continuous installation is the corpus's own.

<OUTSIDE>
The standard legal-history reading differs from the corpus's on one load-bearing point, and it is worth knowing where.

Johnson v. McIntosh is conventionally read as *domesticating* a European inter-sovereign rule rather than importing papal authority as such. Marshall's argument is that discovery gave the discovering nation title good against other European nations — a rule about which colonizer could deal with a given territory — and that the United States succeeded to Britain's position. Robert Miller and Steven Newcomb read the continuity with the bulls much as the corpus does; Eric Kades and others read the doctrine as a monopsony device whose function was to suppress the price of land by eliminating competing buyers, which is closer to the corpus's own "federal land monopsony" phrasing than to its papal-descent framing. Both readings survive the same text.

The mechanism the corpus does not track is what happened after 1823. Cherokee Nation (1831) and Worcester (1832) — which the corpus does hold — are the first two of what became the Marshall Trilogy, and the doctrine's operative modern form runs through *plenary power* (Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 1903) and the trust relationship, not through the bulls directly. That is the administrative machinery this corpus is not built to index, and it is where a present-day title argument would actually have to be fought.

On the Moroccan treaty: it is genuinely the longest continuously in-force US treaty, and the corpus is right that the 1952 ICJ case adjudicated only its commercial provisions. What it does not say is that the treaty is a bilateral instrument between two states — it establishes obligations between the US and Morocco, and does not on its face confer standing on private individuals asserting descent. That gap is precisely the "sovereignty provisions were never tested" point the corpus makes at [E-W6-010-01], and it is a real open question rather than a settled one in either direction.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1095, 1209, 1452, 1455, 1456, 1479, 1492, 1493, 1494, 1496, 1513, 1606, 1750, 1765, 1769, 1787, 1823, 2023
</YEARS>

triage.summary: The corpus's claim that Moroccan sovereignty provisions in the 1787 treaty were 'never tested' requires qualification: the treaty establishes bilateral state obligations, not private standing, which is a structural legal gap rather than an open question awaiting adjudication.
triage.note: The answer itself is well-evidenced on the chain 1095–1823 and correctly identifies the corpus's frame. The outside commentary identifies a real constraint: the corpus tracks the papal-descent narrative through Marshall but not the post-1823 administrative machinery (plenary power, trust relationship) where modern title disputes actually run. The Moroccan material is genuinely novel to the corpus and correctly cited, but the standing question at E-W6-010-01 conflates 'never tested in court' with 'open question' — the treaty's bilateral structure answers it structurally without litigation. The operator should decide whether the corpus's framing of that entry oversells the sovereignty claim's present viability.

trigger_context: Explain the Requerimiento to me. Did anyone think it was real?
raw_content:
The Requerimiento was drafted by Juan López de Palacios Rubios, a crown jurist, and promulgated in 1513. It was a document conquistadors were legally required to read aloud before attacking an indigenous population. Its content is a compressed history of the world: God made the earth, Peter and his successors hold authority over it, one such successor granted these lands to the crown of Castile — the reference is to Inter Caetera, twenty years earlier [E-W1-010-01] — and you are therefore already subjects. Accept this, and you will be received in love. Refuse, and the deaths and losses that follow are your own fault and not the crown's.

The corpus files it under T-DISCOVERY-DOCTRINE as the layer between the papal grant and the encomienda, and its operative detail is the mechanical one: it was read in Spanish, to Spanish-illiterate populations, and refusal *or non-response* constituted casus belli [E-W1-015-02], [E-W1-015-01]. That last clause is the whole machine. There is no available answer that is not consent. Silence is refusal, refusal is just cause, and the document has manufactured the legal predicate for whatever happens next before anything has happened.

The corpus calls this "consent theater" — its own phrase, not a term from the scholarship [E-W1-015-03] — and links it forward to nineteenth-century Native treaty consent fictions and to modern disclosure-and-consent architectures [E-W1-015-01]. I would add the structural pairing the corpus keeps in separate entries: the Capitulations of Santa Fe granted Columbus title and viceroyalty over lands not yet reached, in April 1492, before any contact [E-W1-009-02]. So the sequence is title issued before arrival, then consent demanded after arrival, with the consent shaped so it cannot be withheld. The paperwork is complete in both directions and at no point does it require the participation of anyone on the land.

On your actual question — did anyone think it was real — the corpus's answer is oblique but pointed. It does not carry the contemporary reactions directly. What it carries is the argument the Spanish had with themselves at Valladolid in 1550, and the tell is what Sepúlveda, arguing *for* the wars, would not say. He grounds just cause in Aristotelian natural slavery, in punishing sins against nature, in rescuing sacrifice victims, in clearing the way for preaching — and "explicitly denies that mere disbelief is a just cause" [E-W1-019-02]. The Requerimiento's entire premise is that non-submission to a papal grant is a just cause. The most aggressive defender of the conquest available, thirty-seven years later, is arguing on grounds that concede the document's logic does not hold.

The corpus makes this sharper in an entry it marks clearly as its own inference rather than a quotation from any primary source: the Salamanca just-war tradition distinguished the invincibly ignorant, who had never encountered the Gospel, from the culpable rejecter who knew and refused — and the Requerimiento "asserts only blanket papal jurisdiction," collapsing a distinction the managers' own theology had drawn [E-W1-034-01]. That entry is tier C and says so. But it identifies the defect precisely: the document does theological work its authors' own theology did not license.

And Valladolid itself is the confirmation that nobody was really adjudicating this. No indigenous participants, no binding verdict, one judge still unruled by 1557, and colonial extraction continuing unchanged — the corpus says the forensic value is the justification-versus-practice split, not a policy hinge [E-W1-019-02]. The same split the Requerimiento embodies in miniature.

<OUTSIDE>
The contemporary reaction is documented and it is close to universal derision, which the corpus does not carry.

Las Casas wrote that he did not know whether to laugh or weep at the thing. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo — a royal official, not a critic of the conquest — recorded reading it and then asking a colleague whether anyone's conscience was actually satisfied by it. The practices that grew up around it are the real evidence: it was read from shipboard out of earshot, to empty villages whose inhabitants had fled, to stands of trees, at night to sleeping settlements, and frequently mumbled to a notary rather than to anyone else, because what mattered was the notarial attestation that it had been read. It was a document addressed to a file, not to a people.

Two pieces of context that change how it reads. It came out of a crisis of conscience rather than out of confidence: Antonio de Montesinos preached at Hispaniola in Advent 1511 asking "are these not men?", which forced Ferdinand to convene the Burgos junta, which produced the Laws of Burgos in 1512 and the Requerimiento the following year. It is a legitimation document written because the legitimacy had been publicly challenged from a pulpit by a Dominican. And its form has a probable Islamic model — the da'wa, the formal summons to accept Islam that jurists required before lawful attack. Palacios Rubios was working in a Castile that had absorbed centuries of that legal tradition, which the corpus's own Iberian window would recognise.

It did not survive long as policy. The New Laws of 1542 curtailed the encomienda, and Philip II's Ordenanzas of 1573 removed the word "conquest" from official vocabulary in favour of "pacification," by which point the Requerimiento had already fallen out of use. It was abandoned not because it failed but because it had become embarrassing — which is a different thing from being found unlawful, and the underlying title claim it served was never disturbed.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1492, 1493, 1511, 1512, 1513, 1550
</YEARS>

triage.summary: Contemporary Spanish responses to the Requerimiento document universal derision and evidence of bad faith in its application—read out of earshot, to empty villages, at night, mumbled to notaries rather than audiences—indicating its drafters and enforcers knew its legal logic was not genuinely persuasive.
triage.note: The OUTSIDE material documents Las Casas and Oviedo as primary sources for contemporary rejection of the document's premise; the corpus already carries the Valladolid argument (Sepúlveda's refusal to justify conquest on Requerimiento grounds) as indirect evidence of its invalidity, but lacks the direct contemporary derision. The historical context—that it emerged from Montesinos's 1511 pulpit challenge, forcing legitimation through a document—explains why the Requerimiento exists at all as an anxiety response rather than a confident instrument. The Islamic da'wa model suggests the form was borrowed from Castile's own legal tradition, placing it in a deeper genealogy. The practical abandonement under Philip II (not as unlawful but as embarrassing) is a separate finding: the title claim it served was never disturbed even after the document fell away, suggesting the Requerimiento was always secondary to prior title assertion (the Capitulations sequence the answer already notes).

trigger_context: Two papal bulls in 1452 and 1455 keep coming up. What's the difference between them?
raw_content:
Three real differences, and the corpus is tier A on all of it.

**What kind of instrument each is.** Dum Diversas, 18 June 1452, is a grant of *faculty* — Nicholas V gives Alfonso V "full and free faculty to invade, conquer, subdue and reduce to perpetual servitude the Saracens, pagans, and any other unbelievers and enemies of Christ wheresoever placed," and to seize their kingdoms, possessions and goods [E-W1-001-01]. It is a licence to act. Romanus Pontifex, 8 January 1455, is a charter: the corpus describes it as expanding Dum Diversas "into a comprehensive colonial charter for Portugal" [E-W1-003-02]. One authorises conduct; the other constitutes a jurisdiction.

**Scope, which moves in opposite directions.** Dum Diversas is geographically unbounded — *wheresoever placed* — and the corpus makes the point that its operative category is therefore defined by jurisdiction to Christendom, not by race or geography [E-W1-001-01]. Romanus Pontifex narrows the map and grants Portugal *exclusive* rights south of Cape Bojador [E-W1-003-03]. So the later bull is geographically tighter but adds something the first lacks: monopoly against other Christian princes. That exclusivity is what the 1479 Alcáçovas partition and eventually Tordesillas are elaborating [E-W1-006-01].

**Perpetual versus hereditary.** This is the substantive one. Dum Diversas says perpetual servitude — a condition fixed for the life of the person subdued. Romanus Pontifex, in the corpus's reading, "explicitly authorizes hereditary slavery" [E-W1-003-01] and reduces the inhabitants of seized pagan lands to that status [E-W1-003-02]. The corpus files this as the bull that "formalizes hereditary-servitude classification principle" and marks it the direct upstream ancestor of the Asiento of 1518 [E-W1-003-01], [E-W1-016-01]. Perpetual binds a person; hereditary creates a category that descends, and a category that descends is a thing you can contract over decades in advance.

I want to flag a connection the corpus does not draw. It carries two separate lines to heritable status: this papal one, running 1455 to the Asiento, and an Iberian one running from the 1449 Toledo blood-purity statute, where "the classification moves from behavior (faith) to biology (blood)" and becomes permanent [E-W0-042-03], through casta and into Virginia's Partus Sequitur Ventrem of 1662, which makes status descend by the mother [E-W2-016-01]. Those are threaded separately — Toledo links forward to Partus, Romanus Pontifex links forward to the Asiento — and putting them side by side as two runs of the same operation is my inference, not the corpus's link.

One caution about the corpus's own text. [E-W1-003-02] says Nicholas V and Calixtus III "jointly issue" Romanus Pontifex, which is loose; Nicholas issued it in January 1455 and died that March, and Calixtus succeeded in April. The corpus's own other entry gives the cleaner sequence and makes the better point with it: Calixtus in 1456 issues his *own* Inter Caetera reaffirming both earlier bulls, which the corpus reads as the structural fact — "papal bulls are institutional software that survives the individual pope's death, reconfirmed across successions" [E-W1-004-02]. Not to be confused with the 1493 Inter Caetera, which is a different bull with the same incipit [E-W1-010-01].

<OUTSIDE>
A bibliographic point that explains why Romanus Pontifex is the one you see quoted. It *recites* Dum Diversas at length — the 1455 bull rehearses the earlier grant before extending it — which the corpus alludes to when it calls Romanus Pontifex a "recital of the same grant" [E-W1-001-01]. Romanus Pontifex entered the standard printed collections and the Portuguese chancery record more securely, and it was read publicly in Lisbon cathedral in 1455 in both Latin and Portuguese. So it is the better-attested text, and modern Discovery Doctrine literature quotes it more or less by default. Frances Gardiner Davenport's *European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States* (1917) is where most English-language citation of both ultimately traces.

The lobbying context is worth knowing because it explains the exclusivity clause. Alfonso V sought confirmation not primarily against non-Christians but against *Castile*, which was contesting Portuguese claims along the African coast. The bulls are as much an intra-European territorial settlement as an authorisation against anyone else — which is precisely the structure Johnson v. McIntosh later reproduces when Marshall holds that discovery gave title good against other European nations.

One caveat on the hereditary reading. The Latin of both bulls speaks of reducing persons to perpetual servitude (*in perpetuam servitutem*), and how much genuinely hereditary status the 1455 text adds beyond that is contested among historians rather than settled — some read the expansion as primarily territorial and commercial, with heritability of status developing in practice through the Atlantic trade rather than being conferred by the bull. The corpus states the hereditary reading flatly at tier A; the scholarship is less unanimous than that.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1449, 1452, 1455, 1456, 1479, 1493, 1518, 1662
</YEARS>

triage.summary: E-W1-003-02 states Nicholas V and Calixtus III 'jointly issue' Romanus Pontifex, but Nicholas issued it in January 1455 and died in March; Calixtus succeeded in April and issued his own reaffirmation (Inter Caetera, 1456) as a separate act. The reconfirmation across papal succession is the structural point, not joint issuance.
triage.note: The corpus already captures the correct sequence and significance in E-W1-004-02 ('papal bulls are institutional software that survives the individual pope's death, reconfirmed across successions'). E-W1-003-02 should align with that framing. Also flagged: historiographical dispute over whether Romanus Pontifex genuinely authorizes hereditary slavery or whether heritability developed in practice through the Atlantic trade — the corpus states the hereditary reading at tier A but scholarship is less unanimous.

trigger_context: How did a line drawn on a map at Tordesillas in 1494 turn into anyone's legal title to land?
raw_content:
It mostly didn't — and the corpus's own entries show why, if you read what the line actually allocates.

Tordesillas is a bilateral instrument. Spain and Portugal agree a meridian 370 leagues west of Cape Verde and divide the world into a western and an eastern half [E-W1-011-01]. What each crown receives is exclusivity *against the other*, which is why the corpus's framework line calls it a bilateral treaty operationalizing Inter Caetera rather than creating anything new [E-W1-011-03]. And the qualifier in the underlying bull gives the game away: Alexander VI grants Spain lands "not already occupied by any Christian prince" [E-W1-010-01]. Cabot's English patent two years later uses the same construction — lands "which before this time were unknown to all Christians" [E-W1-012-02]. The exclusion in every one of these instruments is other European claimants. Inhabitants are not a party to the allocation and are not what the allocation is about.

The corpus supplies the proof of that in one detail. Portugal receives Brazil under the line despite not yet knowing Brazil exists, and formally claims it only in 1500 with Cabral [E-W1-011-01]. You cannot have title to a place you have not identified. What you can have is a prior right to acquire whatever turns out to be there, good against one named rival.

So the line does not produce title. It produces a *monopoly on the right to acquire title*, and separate instruments do the work of converting that into a claim against the people on the ground. The Requerimiento manufactures the consent, with non-response counting as refusal and refusal as just cause [E-W1-015-02]. The encomienda distributes the inhabitants themselves as tribute-and-labour grants — and the corpus is careful that it "did not include a grant of land" [E-W1-013-02]. The Capitulations of Santa Fe had already issued Columbus admiral and viceroy titles over anything discovered, before contact [E-W1-009-02]. Each of these does something the line cannot.

The conversion into land title proper happens in English corporate drafting and then in American law. The 1606 Virginia Charter carries the non-Christian subjugation logic out of papal instrument into ordinary commercial form, and grants land in free and common socage from the Manor at East-Greenwich — the colonists are tenants [E-W2-002-01], [E-W2-002-02]. Then Johnson v. McIntosh in 1823 does the load-bearing move: it reduces indigenous title to a right of occupancy and holds that only the federal government may purchase [E-W4-027-02]. The corpus's own gloss on that is the sharpest thing in the chain — "the government buys at the lowest possible price from peoples who have no alternative buyer" [E-W4-027-01].

That is where I would put the answer, and I am stating it as my reading rather than the corpus's: the line never became title to land. It became a rule about who may buy, and three centuries later that rule was inherited as a monopsony that set the purchase price at near nothing. Title was still acquired by purchase or conquest. What the Discovery instruments removed was the possibility of a competing bidder.

Two further things the corpus lets you see. First, the same operation runs twice: Alcáçovas in 1479 is a bilateral partition subsequently ratified by papal bull in 1481 [E-W1-006-01], and Tordesillas is a bilateral partition subsequently ratified by Julius II in 1506 [E-W1-011-01]. In both cases the crowns settle it between themselves and the papal instrument arrives afterward to bless what has been agreed — which is the reverse of the direction the doctrine is usually narrated as flowing.

Second, the line binds only its signatories. Henry VII issues Cabot's patent in 1496 as the first Northern European challenge to the Iberian monopoly [E-W1-012-01], and Elizabeth grants Raleigh a patent in 1584 for lands "not actually possessed of any Christian Prince" [E-W1-029-01] — accepting the *form* of the argument while ignoring the Iberian allocation entirely. A partition two parties agree is not law to a third.

<OUTSIDE>
The doctrinal name for what you are describing is the distinction between *imperium* and *dominium* — sovereignty over a territory versus ownership of the soil. Nearly all the confusion in the popular reading of Tordesillas comes from collapsing them. The bulls and the treaty operate on imperium. Ownership of particular parcels came from land grants, purchase, and conquest, which is why Spanish colonial law generated a whole apparatus of *mercedes de tierra* and later *composición de tierras* to sort out who actually held what — machinery this corpus does not track, and which is where real title in Spanish America came from.

The doctrinal challenge arrived quickly and from inside. Francisco de Vitoria, lecturing at Salamanca around 1539, went through the standard justifications for Spanish title and rejected most of them outright, including papal donation — the Pope had no temporal jurisdiction over infidels to give away. He accepted that the Indians were true owners, with dominium, before the Spanish arrived. This is precisely the gap the corpus gestures at when it notes Sepúlveda would not argue from mere disbelief [E-W1-019-02]. The Salamanca critique never dislodged the practice, but it means the "papal donation as source of title" reading was contested by Catholic theologians within fifty years of the bull.

On Marshall in 1823: the doctrine he announces is explicitly a rule of relations among European powers, and he says so — discovery gave title against other Europeans, and the United States succeeded to Britain's position. What is genuinely novel in Johnson is applying an inter-sovereign allocation rule so as to disable the inhabitants' capacity to sell to anyone but the government. Eric Kades's work reads the whole doctrine as a price-suppression device rather than a theory of title, which is close to what the corpus's monopsony entry is saying.

One footnote the corpus's Manila galleon link implies but does not spell out. Tordesillas drew one meridian and left the antimeridian undefined, which produced a genuine legal crisis when both crowns reached the Moluccas from opposite directions. It was resolved by the Treaty of Zaragoza in 1529 — Spain sold its claim to Portugal for 350,000 ducats. A partition line settled by cash, which tells you what these instruments were understood to be worth and what kind of thing they were.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1479, 1481, 1493, 1494, 1496, 1500, 1503, 1506, 1513, 1584, 1606, 1823
</YEARS>

triage.summary: The corpus should explicitly distinguish imperium from dominium across Discovery-era instruments; these allocate sovereignty among European powers, not land title to soil, which required separate mechanisms (grants, purchase, conquest). The line produced a monopsony on purchase rights, not title itself.
triage.note: Answer identifies systematic misreading in how the corpus narrates the doctrine's direction of flow (bilateral settlements precede papal ratification, not vice versa). Also notes: Tordesillas binds only signatories (Cabot and Raleigh patents ignore it); real Spanish colonial title came through mercedes and composición machinery not tracked in corpus; Vitoria's internal Catholic critique of papal donation authority arrived by ~1539; Zaragoza 1529 resolution (Spain selling Moluccan claim for 350,000 ducats) demonstrates what these instruments were understood to be—tradeable monopolies on acquisition rights, not title. The corpus's existing monopsony gloss on Johnson v. McIntosh is sharp but needs framing as the load-bearing move in converting inter-sovereign allocation rules into a price-suppression device against indigenous sellers.

trigger_context: What was the encomienda, and what replaced it when it was abolished?
raw_content:
The premise of "abolished" needs a small correction before the answer works, but the substance is straightforward and the corpus is tier A on both instruments, threading them together as T-THREE-TRACK-LABOR.

The encomienda: forced labour is ordered in the 1501 Ovando instructions — "require the Indians to work in the things of Our service" — practiced from 1502, and formally legalised by royal provision of 20 December 1503 [E-W1-013-02]. Under the fiction of *encomendar*, entrustment for protection and Christianisation, a colonist receives tribute or labour from a set number of people. The detail the corpus insists on, and which matters enormously given how the institution is usually described: it "did not include a grant of land" [E-W1-013-02]. An encomienda is a grant of *people*, or more precisely of a claim on their output. It is not a landholding.

And it is not new. The corpus traces it directly to the Reconquista — tribute exacted from Muslims and Jews during the reconquest of Iberia, re-deployed via the Canaries to the Americas [E-W1-013-02]. The land-redistribution half of that same template had already been rehearsed on conquered Moorish estates handed to Spanish military nobility [E-W0-002-02]. So the two halves of the Iberian operation arrive in the Americas separately: land redistribution as one instrument, tribute-over-persons as another.

What replaced it was the repartimiento, and the corpus does something careful here that is worth carrying over, because the word has three referents that get collapsed. The one that matters is the post-1549 rotational labour draft, in definite form by about 1575: a state-administered forced-labour quota, rotating levies of roughly five per cent to the mines and ten per cent to seasonal agriculture, wages legally required and routinely ignored [E-W1-020-02]. This is the Peruvian *mita* and the New Spain *cuatequil*. Distinguish it from (a) the early 1492–1542 grant the corpus calls "legally distinct but functionally identical" to encomienda, which is the antecedent rather than the successor, and (b) the *repartimiento de mercancías*, a forced goods sale and not a labour system at all [E-W1-020-02].

The corpus reads the substitution plainly as a rebrand: it files the entry as "the rebrand-and-continue operation" and says the coercion persists in practice past the 1601 and 1609 reforms [E-W1-020-02], [E-W1-020-03]. What actually changed is the operator. Encomienda vests the claim in a private colonist; repartimiento vests it in the state, which then allocates. Same extraction, moved from private grant to administrative draft — the corpus's own framing.

Two things worth marking about evidentiary weight. The corpus proposes the repartimiento as a structural template for the Thirteenth Amendment's convict-leasing exception and modern labour classification, and explicitly flags this down as analogy held at H3, "not asserted by the repartimiento scholarship" [E-W1-020-01]. Take that as the corpus arguing, not reporting. By contrast the runtime tail is sourced and hard: Dell (2010) finds the mita boundary still predicts about 25 per cent lower household consumption and about six points higher child stunting today [E-W1-020-02].

And the reform politics sit right beside this. Valladolid convenes in 1550, in the same window, and the corpus's verdict is that Las Casas wins the argument while "colonial extraction continues unchanged" — the forensic value being the justification-versus-practice split rather than any policy hinge [E-W1-019-02]. The repartimiento is that split made operational.

<OUTSIDE>
On "abolished" — the encomienda was never cleanly abolished, and the messiness is the interesting part. The New Laws of 1542 barred new grants and made existing ones non-heritable, which was meant to extinguish the institution by attrition within a generation. The response was armed revolt: Gonzalo Pizarro's rebellion in Peru killed the viceroy sent to enforce them, and the inheritance provisions were repealed in 1545. Encomiendas survived into the eighteenth century and were formally ended in New Spain only in 1720. So the corpus's picture of a 1550s succession is right about where the *centre of gravity* moved, but the two systems overlapped for a very long time.

Two mechanisms the corpus does not track that explain why the shift happened at all. First, demographic collapse — the indigenous population of central Mexico fell by something like ninety per cent across the sixteenth century, which made fixed per-encomendero allocations unworkable and pushed the crown toward a rotating draft that could ration a shrinking labour pool. Second, the crown had its own reason to prefer the repartimiento independent of any reform impulse: encomenderos were becoming a hereditary colonial aristocracy with private claims on population, which is exactly the kind of intermediate power a centralising monarchy dislikes. Moving the allocation into royal officials' hands was as much a jurisdictional consolidation as a humanitarian one.

The Potosí mita is the extreme case and the one Dell studies: sixteen highland provinces obliged to send one seventh of adult men annually to the silver mines, a system running from Viceroy Toledo's reforms of the 1570s until 1812. It is also the mechanism by which the American silver in the corpus's Manila galleon and Piet Hein entries was actually produced.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1501, 1502, 1503, 1542, 1545, 1549, 1550, 1575, 1601, 1609, 1720
</YEARS>

triage.summary: The corpus's repartimiento entry omits two structural drivers of the encomienda-to-repartimiento shift: demographic collapse of the indigenous population (which made fixed allocations unworkable) and crown preference for jurisdictional consolidation over private colonial aristocracy, both independent of reform impulse. The answer also flags that encomienda and repartimiento overlapped for ~170 years rather than succeeding cleanly, with the crown's own centralising interest as operative motive alongside—or prior to—humanitarian argument.
triage.note: The 'abolished' premise is worth tracking as a corpus design issue: the entry may be stating or implying cleaner discontinuity than the historical record supports. The Potosí mita (1570s–1812) is the corpus's own mechanism for American silver production in Manila galleon and Piet Hein entries, suggesting the repartimiento material should thread those connections more explicitly. Dell (2010) runtime tail on mita boundary effects (25% consumption/6pt stunting) is already in corpus; the two omitted mechanisms are causal structure the corpus does not carry.

trigger_context: Explain partus sequitur ventrem and why 1662 matters.
raw_content:
The statute is Act XII of the Virginia General Assembly, December 1662: "all children borne in this country shalbe held bond or free only according to the condition of the mother" [E-W2-016-01]. That single clause reverses the common-law presumption that status descended from the father. What makes it load-bearing rather than merely tidy is the corpus's own framing of the effect — the classification "stops depending on any act, contract or belief of the person classified and begins descending by birth" [E-W2-016-02].

Why 1662 rather than some other year: because of what happened in 1656, and the corpus threads these directly. Elizabeth Key was the daughter of an English planter, Thomas Key, and an enslaved African woman. When John Mottrom's estate was settled in 1655 she was inventoried as "Elizabeth the Negro woman & her sonne." She sued on three grounds — paternal status at common law, Christian baptism, and an expired nine-year indenture — and won, the Assembly finding that "the Child of a Woman slave begott by a free-man ought to bee free" [E-W2-013-01]. The corpus titles that entry "THE EXIT DOOR THAT TRIGGERS PARTUS." I would note the tier discipline here: the corpus marks the statute itself as Proven and Key-as-prompting-cause as only Supported, with the warrant explicitly Open on "what prompted it" [E-W2-016-02]. So the sequence is documented; the causation is the corpus's reading, held rather than asserted.

Now look at what Key's three grounds were, and what happens to each. Paternity closes in 1662. Baptism closes in 1667, when the Assembly enacts that "the conferring of baptisme doth not alter the condition of the person as to his bondage or ffreedome," reasoning that masters may now "endeavour the propagation of christianity" without risking their property [E-W2-042-01]. The indenture ground closes structurally — an indenture is a term, and there is no term when status is inherited at birth. Three exits, three closures, eleven years. That the doors close one at a time in exactly the order Key raised them is my observation, not something the corpus states, but the entries themselves supply every piece of it.

Then it consolidates. In 1682 Virginia merges "Negroes, Moors, Mollattoes or Indians" whose parentage and native country are not Christian into a single enslaveable category, with later conversion no bar [E-W2-027-01]. In 1705 four decades of piecemeal statute are compiled into one code, and the corpus reads that as the moment the classification is "no longer assembled per dispute but issued as law" [E-W2-044-02].

The doctrinal ancestry the corpus draws is Iberian. The 1449 Toledo blood-purity statute is where "the classification moves from behavior (faith) to biology (blood)" and becomes permanent, and that entry links forward to Partus by name [E-W0-042-03]. The corpus calls Toledo the doctrinal source and Partus the American execution [E-W0-042-02]. Same move, two centuries and an ocean apart, with the difference that Toledo works through genealogical audit of ancestry [E-W0-042-04] and Partus needs no audit at all — you only have to know who the mother was.
outside:
The phrase is Roman. *Partus sequitur ventrem*, the offspring follows the belly, was a rule of property in the *ius gentium* governing increase — the calf belongs to the owner of the cow — and it also governed the status of children born to enslaved women under Roman law. Virginia's drafters were reaching for a maxim that already carried both meanings at once, which is precisely what they needed: a rule about the reproduction of property that also determined the legal condition of persons.

Virginia was the first English colony to enact it, and the other colonies followed rather than converged independently. Maryland is the instructive counter-case. In 1664 it went the opposite way, providing that children of English women and enslaved men would follow the *father* into servitude — intended to deter such unions, but it created a perverse incentive for masters to encourage them, since it generated enslaved children from free English mothers. Maryland reversed to the maternal rule in 1681. The experiment ran for seventeen years and was abandoned as unworkable, which tells you the maternal rule was chosen for function rather than inherited doctrine.

The economic consequence is the one usually named as decisive: it makes the enslaved population self-reproducing. Increase becomes an asset generated internally rather than purchased, which over the long run made the North American system demographically distinct from the Caribbean and Brazilian systems, where mortality outran birth and continuous importation was structurally required. That distinction is why the United States could end the transatlantic trade in 1808 without the institution contracting.

One legal point worth being exact about: the statute's real work is that it makes the *father's* identity legally irrelevant. Under *pater est quem nuptiae demonstrant* paternity mattered and could be litigated, as Key litigated it. After 1662 a white father has no status to transmit and, correspondingly, nothing to answer for. The rule that made enslavement heritable is the same rule that made paternity by an enslaver legally invisible.
</OUTSIDE>

trigger_context: What did the Royal African Company actually do, at what scale?
raw_content:
The Royal African Company was chartered 27 September 1672 by Charles II, superseding the surrendered 1663 Company of Royal Adventurers, whose governor since 1660 had been James, Duke of York — the King's brother [E-W2-023-01], [E-W2-014-01]. James kept the governorship and became James II in 1685, so for a stretch the sitting monarch of England was head of the chartered slaving monopoly [E-W2-028-01]. That is not a coincidence to be explained; it is what the charter was for. The Crown entering the African trade at the ownership level is how the corpus reads the 1660 predecessor [E-W2-014-01].

What it did, mechanically: monopoly on English trade with West Africa — gold from the Gold Coast alongside the slave infrastructure [E-W2-023-03] — with captives branded DY for the Duke, or RAC on the chest [E-W2-023-01].

The scale, which the corpus gives in two different measures. During the monopoly years 1672 to 1689 the Company shipped roughly 5,000 enslaved people a year, about twenty-three voyages annually, 90,000 to 100,000 people in total, mainly to the Caribbean and Virginia [E-W2-023-01]. Across the longer span 1672 to 1731 it invested in voyages carrying 186,748 people, of whom 16,077 died at sea [E-W2-023-01]. That second pair of figures is the more useful one, because it is a count of investment rather than of direct operation, and because the mortality figure is stated separately — roughly one in twelve, recorded as a line item.

The corpus reads this as "the Software layer at industrial scale," converting people into "branded, insured, accounted cargo" [E-W2-023-02]. The insurance half of that is a real and separate apparatus: by the 1690s slave voyages are routinely underwritten at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse on Tower Street, converting the classified into actuarial products, each voyage a priced portfolio of shipwreck, mutiny, disease and mortality risk [E-W2-031-01]. Worth noting the corpus's own honesty on tier — the RAC entries are tier A and the assessment marks the charter and volumes as Proven but Pettigrew's superlative as merely Attributed [E-W2-023-02].

The most interesting thing about the Company, though, is what happened when it lost its monopoly.

In 1698 Parliament opened the African trade to private merchants on a ten per cent duty. Within a decade the separate traders were carrying several times the Company's volume [E-W2-038-01]. The corpus's line on this is the one to keep: "the extraction function disperses from one chartered company to a whole market, and decentralising it raises its throughput rather than lowering it" [E-W2-038-01]. Ending the monopoly did not end the trade. It multiplied it. The corpus files that under the N1 collapse-survival pattern — the wrapper fails, the franchise persists [E-W2-038-01].

That pattern is why the RAC's institutional identity matters less than one might assume. The corpus shows the same trade running under four different kinds of operator in the same century: a crown monopoly here; a private market after 1698; the Dutch WIC under a chartered Atlantic monopoly, at least 265,000 people across its two monopoly periods [E-W2-006-01]; and a *church* — the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel inherits the Codrington plantation in Barbados in 1710, 300-plus people branded SOCIETY on their chests [E-W2-040-01]. The corpus's framing on that last one is exact: "the same classification run not by a state or a company but by a church" [E-W2-040-02].

I would put it this way, and this is my inference rather than a claim the corpus makes: the RAC is best understood not as the cause of anything but as one operator among four, and the 1698 deregulation is the cleanest natural experiment in the window for showing that the classification, not the company, was the load-bearing part.

<OUTSIDE>
Two things worth knowing that the corpus does not carry.

The RAC's own trade was always a minority of the English total even during its monopoly, because interlopers — private traders sailing in defiance of the charter — were substantial from the 1670s onward and repeatedly litigated. The 1698 Act was in part a recognition of a market that already existed illegally. William Pettigrew's *Freedom's Debt* (2013) makes the sharper argument that the separate traders won the political fight by deploying an explicitly *liberal* rhetoric of free trade against monopoly, so the expansion of the slave trade was argued for in the language of English liberty. That is the finding underneath the corpus's throughput observation.

On the DY brand: the corpus's figures come from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org), which is the standard quantitative source for all of this and lets you check company-level totals directly.

And the RAC did not vanish. It limped on with parliamentary subsidies to maintain the West African forts, was dissolved in 1752, and its forts and assets passed to the African Company of Merchants — a regulated rather than joint-stock body, which then administered them until 1821 when the Crown took them over directly. So the physical infrastructure outlasted three successive institutional owners, which is the corpus's N1 pattern running on the buildings rather than the trade.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1660, 1663, 1672, 1685, 1689, 1698, 1710, 1731, 1752
</YEARS>

trigger_context: Bacon's Rebellion is usually taught as a class uprising. What does the corpus make of it?
raw_content:
The corpus does read it broadly the way you were taught — but it flags its own reading as contested, which is the more useful thing about the entry.

The description: a multiracial uprising of indentured servants and enslaved people against the Virginia elite, white and Black labourers united against the planter class, and the Managers' response being to divide the labour pool by race, with the 1682 and 1705 codes as "the direct legislative response to this moment" [E-W2-025-01]. Jamestown burned; the corpus files the takeaway as "the lesson: unified labor = threat" [E-W2-025-02], [E-W2-025-03]. It sits on two threads, T-CHESAPEAKE-CLASS-SPLIT and T-WHITENING-PROJECT.

Now the assessment line, which is where the honesty is. The rising and its composition are marked Proven. The causal line to the racial codes is marked **Contested, per Morgan**, and the warrant is split: Closed on events, **Open on whether the codes were a designed response** [E-W2-025-02]. So the corpus is carrying the standard thesis while recording that its own load-bearing claim is unsettled. That is a live question, not a finding.

I think the corpus is right to hold it open, and its own chronology is why. Lay the classification entries out by date and the hardening is clearly underway well before 1676. John Punch receives lifetime servitude where two European servants receive extended indentures — 1640, thirty-six years earlier, and the corpus calls it the first documented racial sentencing differential in the English colonies [E-W2-010-01]. Johnson v. Casor declares a person property without a crime in 1655 [E-W2-011-02]. Barbados passes the first comprehensive English slave code in 1661, twenty-three clauses, and the corpus notes the template travels — Jamaica 1664, South Carolina 1691 [E-W2-015-01]. Partus makes status heritable in 1662, fourteen years before Bacon [E-W2-016-01]. Baptism is closed as an exit in 1667 [E-W2-042-01]. Anthony Johnson's estate is escheated in 1670 on the finding that he "was a negro and by consequence an alien" [E-W2-022-01].

That is six instruments in the thirty-six years before the rebellion, running in one direction. I am putting these next to Bacon myself; the corpus keeps them as separate entries and does not draw this line. But it seems to me the sequence makes the strong version of the thesis hard to sustain. 1682 and 1705 look less like a *response* to 1676 and more like the continuation of something already well advanced — and the corpus itself describes 1705 not as an innovation but as the compilation of four decades of piecemeal statute into a single code, the classification "no longer assembled per dispute but issued as law" [E-W2-044-02].

There is also the matter of what else 1676 sits beside. King Philip's War runs 1675–1678 in New England, and the corpus reads it as territorial clearing and labour conversion arriving as one operation, with surrendering Indians sold into slavery [E-W2-024-02]. The two are linked in the corpus's own graph. A Virginia-specific story about Bacon has to account for a simultaneous, differently-shaped crisis three hundred miles north.

A weaker and, I think, defensible version survives all of this: 1676 was a demonstration of what an unsegmented labour force could do, and it hardened an existing project rather than originating one. The corpus's own framework language points that way when it calls the event "the trigger for the Chesapeake class split" [E-W2-025-02] — a trigger acts on something already loaded.

<OUTSIDE>
The Morgan the assessment cites is Edmund Morgan, *American Slavery, American Freedom* (1975), and it is worth being clear that Morgan is the *source* of the thesis rather than a critic of it — he argued that Virginia's elite resolved the problem of a dangerous free white underclass by binding them to slavery through race. So the corpus flagging the claim "per Morgan" as contested is really flagging the subsequent literature's response to Morgan.

That response has been substantial. The sharpest objection is the timing one: the demographic shift from indentured English servants to enslaved Africans in the Chesapeake was driven by falling English mortality and rising English wages, which shrank the supply of servants willing to emigrate, and by the collapse of the RAC monopoly after 1698 making Africans cheaper and more available. Russell Menard and others have pressed this hard — the labour transition looks economically determined and was already visible in the 1670s. On that account the codes follow the changing composition of the workforce rather than a political decision to split it.

There is also a documentary problem Morgan's critics raise: no Virginia legislator left a record saying anything like "let us divide them by race." The design claim is inferred from outcome. That is precisely the gap the corpus's "Open" warrant is marking.

Where Morgan still has real force is on the *counterfactual* — Virginia in 1676 did have armed poor whites and enslaved Africans fighting together, it did not thereafter, and the statutory record shows deliberate attention to keeping them apart. Whether that is causation or convergence is genuinely unresolved, and the honest position is the one the corpus takes.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1640, 1655, 1661, 1662, 1667, 1670, 1675, 1676, 1682, 1698, 1705
</YEARS>

triage.summary: The corpus should draw an explicit correlation between the six pre-1676 racial-status instruments (Punch 1640, Johnson v. Casor 1655, Barbados code 1661, Partus 1662, Baptism closure 1667, Anthony Johnson escheat 1670) and the post-Bacon codes, positioning 1676 as acceleration of an existing trajectory rather than origination of the racial-labour split project. The current framework treats these as separate entries; they form a sequence that reshapes the causal claim.
triage.note: The corpus's own 'trigger' language (E-W2-025-02) already points toward this reading — a trigger acts on something loaded. The Morgan thesis rests on a design inference with no documentary warrant; the economic-supply explanation (Menard et al.) is also inference-based. The honest position is that 1676 *demonstrably* hardened existing practice, but whether it *caused* the shift or merely coincided with market-driven labour substitution remains open. King Philip's War simultaneity (E-W2-024-02) also deserves explicit threading. The 1705 entry correctly notes compilation rather than innovation; the pre-1676 sequence makes that reading stronger.

trigger_context: Were there successful counter-moves in this period, or is it all one direction?
raw_content:
Not one direction, no — the corpus runs counter-move as a lane of its own, and threads several of these as T-COLLAPSE-SURVIVAL-N1. But the successes have a shape worth naming, and it is not the shape you would expect.

The clearest one is the Pueblo Revolt. On 10 August 1680 Popé of San Juan leads an almost universal Pueblo uprising; Governor Otermín and the Spanish flee Santa Fe by 21 August. About 400 die, including 21 of the province's 33 Franciscan friars — roughly a quarter of New Mexico's Spanish population — and some 2,000 survivors retreat to El Paso [E-W2-026-01]. The corpus is careful about what makes this different from a temporary rout: a Spanish force of 300 is repelled in 1681, so the twelve years are *defended, not merely uncontested*, until Vargas reconquers in 1692 [E-W2-026-01]. Spanish jurisdiction is voided outright for twelve years and Pueblo territory restored [E-W2-026-03], [E-W2-026-04]. The corpus's framing: "not flight or accommodation but the outright removal of the colonial administration from the province, and the defence of that removal against return" [E-W2-026-02].

The Maroons are the durable case. When the Spanish flee the English conquest of Jamaica in 1655, the people they held take their own freedom and coalesce in the interior. They hold their ground by force until the treaties of 1739 and 1740 acknowledge their autonomy and land — in exchange for military service and the return of later runaways [E-W2-012-01]. Sovereignty acknowledged by the colonial power itself [E-W2-012-02]. The corpus reads this as "escape as the founding of a self-governing polity the colonial power is forced to treat with" [E-W2-012-02]. Note the price in that treaty clause, though. It is a real victory bought by becoming an instrument of the system for everyone who came after.

Then there is a category the corpus keeps returning to, which is my nomination for the most instructive: **counter-moves that work by exploiting the seam between two Managers rather than by defeating one.**

Spain's *cédula real* of 1693 grants freedom to any enslaved person reaching Spanish Florida who converts to Catholicism [E-W2-035-01]. The corpus calls this a jurisdictional instrument — "the same person classified as 'Negro' property under English law becomes FREE under Spanish law by crossing a territorial boundary" [E-W2-035-01] — and files it as "one empire's classification is escaped through the gap between it and a rival empire's" [E-W2-035-02]. It becomes physical at Fort Mose in 1738, a fortified free-Black settlement two miles north of St Augustine, roughly 100 residents [w3-1738-land]. The corpus is blunt that Spain's motive was not moral: the grant is "a diplomatic weapon against the English slave-plantation economy," and the English attack on Fort Mose in 1745 proves it mattered enough to require a military answer [w3-1738-counter-move].

The same logic runs at the top of the political order. In March 1718 Emperor Brim of Coweta convenes Britain, France and Spain and secures a mutual neutrality binding all three simultaneously — it holds for 45 years, until the 1763 Treaty of Paris [w3-1718-sovereign]. Muscogee autonomy preserved against three colonial systems at once by playing them against each other. The corpus notes it collapses the moment the multi-power context does: 1763 eliminates France and forces a bilateral posture [w3-1763-legal].

And Somerset v. Stewart, 1772: Mansfield holds that no positive law of England authorises slavery, so Somerset cannot be held as chattel in English jurisdiction [w3-1772-legal]. The corpus is precise that this abolishes nothing colonial — it produces a jurisdictional alternative *inside* one empire, metropole against colony [w3-1772-counter-move]. Its own summary of all three: "the person does not change, the applicable jurisdiction does" [w3-1772-counter-move].

That is the pattern, and it is the corpus's own — it explicitly groups Coweta, Fort Mose and Somerset as three variants of one strategy [w3-1772-counter-move]. What I would add, as my inference rather than the corpus's: every counter-move that *held* in this period worked on jurisdiction, and every counter-move that worked on the classification itself failed. Elizabeth Key wins her freedom in 1656 on paternity, baptism and expired indenture [E-W2-013-01] — and within eleven years all three grounds are legislated shut [E-W2-016-01], [E-W2-042-01]. The Germantown Quaker petition of 1688, the first public antislavery document in the English colonies, is neither adopted nor rejected by the meeting and disappears into the archives for 150 years [E-W2-030-02]. Winning inside the framework got the framework amended. Stepping outside its jurisdiction got results.

The limits are real, though. Pueblo autonomy lasts twelve years. Coweta lasts 45 and dies with the balance of power that sustained it. Maroon sovereignty survives by contracting to return other people's freedom. None of these reverses the direction of the century — they carve out durable exceptions within it, which is a different and smaller thing.

triage.summary: The corpus groups Coweta (1718), Fort Mose (1738), and Somerset (1772) as variants of a single counter-move strategy—exploiting jurisdictional seams between rival managers rather than defeating one—and the respondent identifies a metalevel pattern: successful counter-moves in this period worked on jurisdiction, while those targeting classification itself were legislated shut within years. This pattern (jurisdiction-based holds, classification-based fails) is both an inference from and a clarification of the corpus's own grouping.
triage.note: The respondent's distinction between 'durable exceptions within the direction' versus 'reversal of the direction' may also warrant explicit framing in the corpus itself. Elizabeth Key (1656) and Germantown (1688) are existing entries; their closure within 11 and 150 years respectively is already tracked but may benefit from explicit connection to the jurisdiction/classification divide.

trigger_context: Virginia's 1705 code is described as making something permanent. Permanent compared to what?
raw_content:
Compared to four specific exits, each of which had previously existed and each of which is named in the corpus's own summary of the code: it reaches "servitude by birth, sealed against **crime, contract and conversion** alike" [E-W2-044-01]. Add paternity and you have the full set.

Take them in order of closure.

**Crime.** In 1640 John Punch receives lifetime servitude where two European fellow-escapees receive extended indentures [E-W2-010-01] — but the corpus is precise that origin is here "operating as a sentencing variable, **still bounded by an underlying offence**" [E-W2-010-02]. Servitude was something you were sentenced to. That gate comes off in 1655, when Johnson v. Casor becomes the "first civil case declaring a person property WITHOUT A CRIME" [E-W2-011-02].

**Paternity.** Common law ran status through the father, which is one of the three grounds Elizabeth Key wins on in 1656 [E-W2-013-01]. Reversed by statute in December 1662 [E-W2-016-01].

**Conversion.** Baptism. Also one of Key's grounds. Closed in 1667, with the Assembly reasoning that masters may now "endeavour the propagation of christianity" without risking their property [E-W2-042-01]. The 1682 statute reconfirms it — later conversion no bar [E-W2-027-01].

**Contract.** An indenture is a term, and terms expire; Key's had, after nine years [E-W2-013-01]. This one is closed not by repeal but structurally: once status descends at birth there is no term to run out.

So "permanent" here means *without exit by right* — not by serving out, not by baptism, not by parentage, and not as the discharge of a sentence.

There is a second axis, which is duration across generations rather than within a life, and that is Partus doing the work: the corpus's line is that the classification "stops depending on any act, contract or belief of the person classified and begins descending by birth" [E-W2-016-02].

And a third comparison the corpus draws itself rather than leaving to inference — the 1449 Toledo limpieza statute entry links directly forward to 1705 [E-W0-042-03], and uses the identical word: "the classification moves from behavior (faith) to biology (blood). This is the inflection point: the Adjective becomes PERMANENT" [E-W0-042-03]. Noun and Adjective are the audit's own analytical vocabulary, not terms from the scholarship. The corpus's reading is that Toledo is the doctrinal source and the Virginia statutes the American execution [E-W0-042-02]. Same closure of the conversion route, 213 years and an ocean apart; the difference is that Toledo needed genealogical audit to enforce [E-W0-042-04] and Partus needed only the identity of the mother.

One thing the corpus does not settle: the 1682 statute carried an explicit exemption for "all servants except Turkes and Moores, whilest in amity with his majesty," turning on diplomatic amity with the Crown rather than Christian status [E-W2-027-01]. Whether that survived the 1705 consolidation is not recorded in the entries here. Given that the corpus's whole Noun-to-Adjective spine turns on the fate of "Moor" as a category, that is a live gap rather than a settled point.

<OUTSIDE>
Worth being precise about what "permanent" does *not* mean, since the corpus doesn't spell it out. The 1705 code sealed the routes out **by right** — the ones a person could claim in court. It did not abolish manumission, which remained a discretionary act of the owner. Virginia restricted that separately and later: a 1723 act required approval by the Governor and Council for meritorious service, the 1782 act liberalised it considerably, and the 1806 act required freed people to leave the state within a year. So the arc runs: close the claimable exits first (1662–1705), then constrain the discretionary one (1723 onward).

The standard term of art for what 1705 completes is **chattel slavery** as distinct from servitude — heritable, lifelong, and treating the person as property transferable by sale and descent. Partus is the technical hinge, and its Latin tag is borrowed from Roman law, where it governed the offspring of livestock. The Barbados code of 1661, which the corpus notes travelled to Jamaica in 1664 and South Carolina in 1691 [E-W2-015-01], had already put the enslaved outside common law as "goods and chattels"; Virginia's route to the same place was slower and more incremental, which is why it leaves the clearer statutory trail.
</OUTSIDE>

<YEARS>
1449, 1640, 1655, 1656, 1662, 1667, 1682, 1705, 1723
</YEARS>

triage.summary: The corpus's characterization of 1705 as establishing "permanent" servitude requires explicit framing as closure of four specific exit routes (crime, paternity, conversion, contract) and should distinguish between elimination of exits-by-right versus later restrictions on discretionary manumission. The framework connecting the Noun-to-Adjective inflection across Toledo (1449) and Virginia (1705) is sound but needs clarification that this describes transition from status-by-act to status-by-birth.
triage.note: A live gap: whether the 1682 statute's exemption for "Turkes and Moores, whilest in amity with his majesty" survived the 1705 consolidation is unrecorded in current entries. This matters because the corpus's analytical spine turns on the fate of "Moor" as a category. Additionally, the answer distinguishes the Virginia route (slower, incremental, leaving clearer statutory trail) from the Barbados/Jamaica/South Carolina route (treating enslaved persons as chattels outside common law by direct declaration), suggesting the corpus may benefit from explicit comparison of mechanisms rather than outcomes alone.

trigger_context: How well evidenced is the 1713 Asiento entry?
raw_content:
Better than most of what surrounds it, and the reason is simple: someone actually opened the contract.

The 1713 material is five entries in one lane-set — [w3-1713-legal] carrying the term and volume, [w3-1713-financial] the per-head duty, [w3-1713-sovereign] the Spanish crown's quarter share, [w3-1713-corporate] the corporate holding, and [w3-1713-records] the conveyance of predecessor concessions. All five rest on the same two sources. The first, the printed Assiento contract itself, is tier A and live_verified, and the dossier records it as read verbatim at Articles I, II, XLII and the Additional Article — which is where the load-bearing figures come from: thirty years commencing 1 May 1713, 4,800 piezas de India a year, 144,000 in total, one composite duty of thirty-three and one third per pieza [w3-1713-legal]. Those are quotations from the instrument, not inferences about it. The second source, Sperling's monograph on the South Sea Company, is tier A but citation_only — identified and never opened. That single fact is why the assessment reads Warrant: Open despite Weight: Proven.

So the honest summary is: the primary is read, the secondary is not, and every quantitative claim traces to the read primary. That is about as solid as this corpus gets.

What makes it worth saying plainly is the contrast with its own neighbours. The entries immediately upstream — [w3-1662-corporate] on the Grillo and Lomellini contract, [w3-1701-sovereign] on the two crowns taking quarter shareholdings at 100,000 livres apiece — are tier B resting on a single encyclopedia reference, with their warrants openly marked "single reference source; no primary or monograph read." The 1518 origin entries [E-W1-016-01] are tier A claims sitting on a live_provisional secondary web source rather than a primary at all. And the South Sea Company's own 1711 incorporation and debt-for-equity conversion [w3-1711-financial] carries **no source line whatsoever**, which is awkward given that the corpus's framework spine describes Track A as installing "via SSC 1713 renewal." The best-evidenced link in that chain is the 1713 contract; the corporate vehicle the spine names is the least.

Two further things I'd want a reader to hold. First, "Track A," the "Three-Track Labor System," and the "domestic Asiento" reading of the 1717 Transportation Act are this audit's analytical vocabulary, not terms from the historiography of the slave trade — the 1713 contract is a real and much-studied instrument, but nobody outside this corpus calls it Track A. Second, and this is me pointing at something the entries let you see rather than something they claim: the read primary actually undercuts any reading of 1713 as an installation date. [w3-1713-records] records that Article XXXIX conveys every concession of six named predecessor asentistas and keeps their orders re-issuable. The contract is drafted as a succession document. Read alongside [w3-1662-corporate], where English companies are already assisting the carriage under a Genoese licence fifty years earlier, and [w3-1701-sovereign], where two crowns hold equity in the operating company, 1713 is a change of licence-holder inside a running franchise. The corpus threads these on T-ASIENTO and T-MERCHANT-BANKER-CONSTANT precisely so that the continuity is visible, and its own strongest source is the one that documents it.
outside: For calibration on the underlying instrument: the Asiento's transfer to Britain at Utrecht is thoroughly worked over in the standard literature, and the figures in this entry are the conventional ones. What that literature adds, and what the corpus does not track, is the gap between contract and performance — the South Sea Company consistently delivered well below its 4,800-per-year entitlement, and much of the commercial value of the Asiento to British merchants lay in the smuggling of manufactured goods it licensed as cover rather than in the slave deliveries themselves. That matters for how you read [w3-1713-financial]: the per-head duty is what the contract priced, not necessarily what the trade earned. Anyone wanting to test the entry further would go to the Company's own records and the Board of Trade correspondence, neither of which appears in this corpus.

triage.summary: The entry w3-1711-financial (South Sea Company 1711 incorporation and debt-for-equity conversion) carries no source line whatsoever, creating a gap in the evidential chain that the corpus's own framework spine identifies as foundational to Track A. This entry requires sourcing before the framework claim about 1713 renewal can stand.
triage.note: The broader audit reveals a structural problem: the corpus uses 1713 as an installation date and analytical anchor, but its strongest primary evidence (the Asiento contract itself) actually documents 1713 as a succession and licence transfer within a running franchise dating to at least 1662. The 'Three-Track Labor System' and 'Track A' terminology are corpus-internal analytical vocabulary, not historiographic terms. The secondary source on the South Sea Company (Sperling) remains unread. Additionally, the standard literature on the Asiento documents a significant gap between contract entitlements (4,800 piezas/year) and actual performance, with smuggling as the real commercial value—material the corpus does not track but should be noted as contextual limitation on w3-1713-financial's interpretation.

trigger_context: Which window is weakest on evidence?
raw_content:
By the corpus's own accounting, Window 5. It is also the largest window, at 188 entries, and those two facts are related — but not in a way that excuses it.

The distinctive thing about W5 is that a large fraction of its entries carry assessment lines that say so outright: "Weight: Asserted (window content, unsourced) | Warrant: Open (bucket unsourced)." You see it at [E-W5-003-01] on the founding of the Children's Aid Society, at [E-W5-007-01] on the Legal Tender Act year, at [E-W5-044-01] on the Jekyll Island meeting, at [E-W5-058-01], at [E-W5-061-01] on the 1929 crash. Where a bucket is partially sourced the entry says that too — [E-W5-041-01] reads "Proven (1 of 6 entries sourced, tier B) · Asserted (5 unsourced)." That is honest bookkeeping and it is the reason I can answer your question at all, but the arithmetic it discloses is bad.

Second, a great deal of W5's information lane rests on tier C sources that are Chronicling America **search queries** rather than documents — src-chronam-plessy-coverage-1896 behind [E-W5-034-02], src-chronam-memphis-coverage-1866 behind [E-W5-012-05], src-chronam-1898-wilmington-displacement behind [E-W5-036-05]. These are marked live_verified, and they genuinely were run, but what a hit-count establishes is coverage volume, not framing. The claims resting on them are usually about framing.

Third, and this is the part I find most creditable and most damning at once: W5 contains several entries where the corpus records that its own source cuts against the claim. [E-W5-010-02] says the Denver-press framing of Sand Creek "IS UNTESTED HERE" because the paper actually reached reported it as an atrocity, and no Denver papers are held. [E-W5-019-04] concedes that the sourced page on Douglass and the Freedman's Bank is dated two months before the collapse and is deferential to him, so the claim that the press made him the face of the failure "is NOT established at this date." [E-W5-005-02] admits the causal link from Know-Nothing print to the Louisville riots "is the corpus's and is not established here." [E-W5-038-03] says the measurement taken "CONTRADICTS the covers-nothing-else claim as written." A window that catches itself four times is a window whose remaining unchecked claims should be read with the same suspicion.

That said, I'd flag a second and quite different weakness that a headcount misses, and this next judgement is mine rather than the corpus's. Window 0 has the opposite pathology: high tier, unread sources. The Templar banking entries [E-W0-001-02], the entire Reconquista set [E-W0-002-03], the First Crusade [E-W0-016-01], the Cathar Crusade [E-W0-018-04], the Templar suppression [E-W0-031-03] are all tier A with **every source citation_only** — identified, never opened. That is a confident claim resting on a monograph nobody in this audit has read. W0 also holds the corpus's two explicit self-negations: [E-W0-010-01], the star-fort mound grid, which carries no source at all and says "Empty beats fabricated," and [E-W0-006-01], the Mali Atlantic crossing, marked HELD-NULL with the note that no sourceable basis exists.

So: W5 is weakest on whether the evidence exists. W0 is weakest on whether anyone looked at it. And the corpus's scope note adds a third consideration that cuts across both — W0, W1 and W4 entries are reconstructed by reverse-parsing generated HTML, while W3 alone is preserved from the live source. Reconstruction is a provenance fact about how the entry reached you, not a claim about the underlying history, but it is worth knowing which windows are transcriptions of a rendering and which are the original record.

triage.summary: The corpus's own assessment lines reveal systematic weakness patterns: Window 5 contains 188 entries with a large fraction marked unsourced or resting on Chronicling America search-volume queries rather than document evidence, plus four self-documented cases where sources contradict the claims; Window 0 pairs high confidence with unread tier-A sources (citation_only status across Templar, Reconquista, and Crusade entries) and contains two explicit self-negations. Additionally, Windows 0, 1, and 4 are reconstructed from rendered HTML rather than preserved from live source, creating a provenance distinction worth flagging.
triage.note: The questioner has identified a diagnostic framework already implicit in the corpus's own markup but not surfaced as a coordinated observation. This reveals three independent weakness categories: evidentiary gaps (W5), unread sourcing (W0), and provenance method (W0/W1/W4 vs W3). The four W5 self-contradictions (E-W5-010-02, E-W5-019-04, E-W5-005-02, E-W5-038-03) deserve elevated scrutiny on all remaining unsourced W5 entries. Consider whether the assessment line system should be reorganized to surface these patterns at audit entry, or whether Windows 0 and 5 warrant priority re-sourcing passes.

trigger_context: Is the corpus's claim about Moroccan recognition of the United States safe to cite publicly?
raw_content:
Split it into four claims, because they are in very different evidential states and only two of them are safe.

**The 1787 treaty exists and was ratified before the Constitution took force.** Safe. [w3-1787-legal] rests on the Avalon Project text of the treaty, live_verified, and the ratification date of 18 July 1787 is on the face of the record. The chronological point that the corpus builds on it — that ratification preceded the Constitution's entry into force, so the treaty attaches to Article VI as an inherited obligation rather than a later one [w3-1787-certification] — is arithmetic on undisputed dates. Cite it.

**The treaty was still being adjudicated in the twentieth century.** Safe, and unusually well sourced. [E-W6-010-01] rests on the ICJ's own case record, live_verified, for the 1952 *Rights of Nationals of the United States in Morocco* judgment. The corpus also supplies its own limiting caveat there, which you should carry with it: only the commercial provisions were adjudicated, and the sovereignty provisions were never tested. That caveat is the difference between a defensible statement and an overreach.

**Morocco was the first nation to recognise American independence, in December 1777.** This is the one I would not put in public without qualification. [w3-1777-certification] is a tier A entry whose two sources — Parker and Roberts — are *both* citation_only. Nobody in this audit opened either. So the claim's confident tier reflects a judgement about the books, not a reading of them. Note also that the corpus is more careful in W3 than in W4: [w3-1777-certification] says the Sultan "de facto" recognised the United States by opening ports, whereas [E-W4-005-01] flattens this into "the first nation to recognize American independence (1777)" — and that W4 entry's only live_verified source is the 1786–87 treaty text, which cannot establish anything about 1777. If you cite the strong form, you are citing an unread monograph through an entry that has substituted a different document for it.
