**The relationship is the longest continuously in force in US history.** Repeated at [E-W5-041-04], which attributes it back to the W4 entry rather than to a source of its own, and that entry's own source is the treaty text. It is a widely made claim and probably true in the sense usually meant, but in this corpus it has no independent footing.

One more thing worth having if you are going to say any of this in public, because it is the first objection you will meet: the corpus documents that none of it is currently operative. [E-W6-030-04] records a measurement across all 395,602 characters of the 2026 *Trump v. Barbara* slip opinion — "Morocco" returns zero, "Barbary" zero, "Sundry" zero, against thirteen for *jus soli*. That is a fact about a document rather than an interpretation, and it is the strongest single thing here: the treaty is real, ratified, litigated at the ICJ, and simply absent from the reasoning of the Court that most recently addressed American birthright citizenship.
outside:
Two pieces of context the corpus does not spell out and that will decide how a public claim lands.

The December 1777 document is usually described in the Barbary scholarship not as a recognition addressed to the United States but as a general declaration opening Moroccan ports to the shipping of several nations, the Americans among them. Whether that constitutes recognition in the diplomatic sense is a genuine interpretive question, and the "first to recognise" formulation has been actively promoted for a century by both governments as a piece of bilateral tradition. It is not a fabrication, but it is a diplomatic commonplace rather than a settled scholarly finding, and an informed reader may push back on exactly that.

The "longest continuously in force" claim is normally stated with a wrinkle the corpus glances at without explaining. The 1786–87 treaty was renegotiated in 1836, and it is the 1836 instrument that has operated since — the corpus actually carries that source at [E-W6-010-01] alongside the ICJ record, without noting what it implies. The standard careful formulation is that the treaty *relationship* is the longest unbroken one, not that a single 1787 text has run untouched for 239 years. If you say the latter, someone will produce the 1836 treaty.

triage.summary: The corpus's claim that Morocco was the first nation to recognize American independence in December 1777 rests entirely on two citation-only sources that have never been opened. The entry flattens a de facto recognition (opening ports) into a formal diplomatic recognition without independent verification, and the W4 version substitutes a 1786–87 treaty text as its only live-verified source, which cannot establish anything about 1777. The claim requires either qualification or source verification before public citation.
triage.note: The December 1777 document is typically described in Barbary scholarship as a general port-opening declaration rather than a directed recognition, making the diplomatic interpretation itself contestable. The "longest continuously in force" claim at E-W5-041-04 similarly lacks independent footing and obscures that the operative instrument is the 1836 renegotiation, not the 1787 original. Entry E-W6-030-04 documents the treaty's absence from Trump v. Barbara despite its formal legal status—a structural observation worth recording. These are three separate problems across the Morocco recognition cluster: sourcing gaps, interpretive inflation, and operative obsolescence not clearly distinguished in the corpus.

trigger_context: Are there places where the corpus is rated more confidently than its evidence supports?
raw_content:
Yes, and there's a recognisable shape to them. Almost all the overclaiming sits in one of three patterns.

**Tier A on unread sources.** This is the largest class and it is structural, not occasional. Nearly all of Window 0's spine — the Templar banking fusion [E-W0-001-02], the Reconquista-as-franchise-acquisition reading [E-W0-002-03], the First Crusade template [E-W0-016-01], Omne Datum Optimum [E-W0-017-02], the Cathar Crusade [E-W0-018-04], the Templar suppression [E-W0-031-03] — is tier A with every source citation_only. Barber, Riley-Smith, Pegg and O'Callaghan are all reputable, so the tier is a defensible judgement about the books; but a reader asking "how well evidenced is this" is asking whether anyone checked, and nobody did. The same pattern recurs in W2 at [E-W2-025-01] on Bacon's Rebellion, which is the load-bearing entry for the Chesapeake Class Split construct and rests entirely on an unopened Morgan.

**Tier A where the source is a secondary web page.** [E-W1-016-02], the 1518 Asiento, is tier A carrying a single source marked live_provisional — a teaching website, not the contract. Compare [w3-1713-legal], also tier A, where the contract itself was read verbatim. Those two entries are the same tier and are not in the same evidential state, and the 1518 one is the origin point of the whole T-ASIENTO thread.

**Tier assigned to the instrument, inference smuggled in beside it.** [E-W2-011-02], Johnson v. Casor, is tier A on a court order book — fine for the ruling. But the entry then carries "First civil case declaring a person property WITHOUT A CRIME," a superlative the order book cannot establish and no comparative survey is cited for. Similarly [E-W0-013-01] on A00 is properly tier A and admirably holds every side of the TMRCA dispute, then adds the *nemo dat* conclusion that no classification can extinguish the lineage — which is a legal argument riding on a genetics paper's tier.

Two more specific ones worth naming. [E-W0-020-01], Magna Carta, is tier A on the verified charter text, and the charter does not protect Jews — but the entry's claim that the signing Plantagenet line is traceable via Burke's Peerage to the US Presidency has no source at all and is a wholly different kind of assertion sitting under the same tier. And [E-W1-023-01] on casta is tier A on Katzew, whom the entry itself uses to *narrow* the claim ("an elite view of how society should be arranged... not a window onto lived reality") and to flag the rigid-enforcement reading as contested. That is the corpus doing the right thing — but the entry is still tier A, so a reader skimming tiers gets a stronger signal than the body supports.

To be fair about the direction of the bias: the corpus also underclaims in places. [E-W5-046-01] on the Federal Reserve Act is tier B while carrying a live_verified Cornell text of the statute itself, which is as good as sourcing gets. So the tier field is noisy in both directions, which is really the underlying finding — **tier here tracks a judgement about the source's authority, not the audit's contact with it, and those two things come apart constantly.** The status flag is the more informative field, and it is the one a reader is least likely to look at.
outside: Two conventions from documentary editing that would resolve most of this. Scholarly editions distinguish *seen* from *cited* — an editor who has handled a manuscript marks it differently from one relying on a prior edition's report, and the distinction is printed, not inferred. This corpus already has that data in the live_verified/citation_only flag; it just doesn't surface it in the tier. Second, the standard practice of separating the *authority* of a witness from the *reliability of the transmission* is exactly the split failing here: Barber is a strong authority, but an unread Barber is a weak transmission, and a single letter cannot carry both.

triage.summary: The tier field conflates source authority with evidence contact, causing systematic overclaiming on unread citations and secondary sources while underclaiming on primary texts. The live_verified/citation_only flag carries the diagnostic information but remains invisible to readers. The corpus should separate these judgements or surface the transmission-reliability distinction in its tier logic.
triage.note: Fourteen specific entries detailed as exemplars of three patterns: Tier A on citation_only sources (Window 0 spine, Bacon's Rebellion), Tier A on secondary web sources (1518 Asiento vs. w3-1713-legal contract), and inferences smuggled under instrument tiers (Johnson v. Casor superlative, Magna Carta precedence claim unsourced, casta narrowed but still Tier A). Documentary editing conventions (seen vs. cited marking, authority vs. transmission split) offer direct repair pathways. Underclaiming also present (Federal Reserve Act tier B on live_verified statute text) confirms noise runs both directions, but the bias systematically inflates confidence in unverified secondary authority.

trigger_context: If I could only read one source to strengthen this corpus, which should it be?
raw_content:
Sperling, *The South Sea Company* — the citation_only source sitting beside the read Assiento contract on all five 1713 entries.

The reasoning is about leverage rather than importance. There are more consequential unread books in here: Barber on the Templars carries most of Window 0's spine, Morgan carries the entire Chesapeake Class Split construct through [E-W2-025-01], Davies and Pettigrew carry the Royal African Company at [E-W2-023-01]. But opening any of those upgrades one region of the corpus. Sperling sits at the junction where three separate problems meet.

First, it is the one unread source whose entry-set is otherwise *already* strong. The five 1713 entries have a read primary, quoted verbatim at four articles, with figures traceable to the instrument [w3-1713-legal]. Their warrant is Open for exactly one reason — "one source held at citation_only." That is the cheapest Open warrant to close in the corpus.

Second, and this is the real argument, it should reach the corpus's largest unsourced hole. [w3-1711-financial] — the South Sea Company's incorporation, its receipt of the Asiento, and the conversion of government debt into company stock — carries **no source line at all**, and it is pointed at from two directions: the insurance-actuarial construct names it, and the W6 dossier on the 2023 regional bank failures [E-W6-041-01] treats it as the origin of the pattern. The framework spine says Track A installs "via SSC 1713 renewal," so the corpus's own stated architecture runs through an entry with nothing under it. A monograph on the South Sea Company is the obvious instrument for that.

Third, it bears directly on the corpus's most load-bearing chronological claim in W3. [w3-1720-financial] argues that the Bubble Act passed in June 1720, three months *before* the September crash, and that this inverts the standard reading of the Act as regulatory response. That entry rests on a Wikipedia page for the statute and an internal timeline file at tier C. If that inversion is right it is one of the better findings here, and it is currently supported worse than almost anything around it. Sperling is the natural place to check both the chronology and what the Company was actually doing across the crash — which is also what [w3-1725-financial] needs, since the claim that carriage *peaked* five years after the crash is the empirical foundation the corpus gives for its whole Collapse-Survival N1 pattern.

So one book closes an Open warrant, sources an unsourced spine entry, and tests two claims the audit has built structure on. Nothing else I can see in the source list does more than one of those.

If you wanted a second, I'd take Ekirch's *Bound for America* — but note that it is already live_verified at [w3-1717-legal], so the Transportation Act side of the labour system is in better shape than the Asiento side. Which is itself worth noticing: the corpus has read the domestic track and not the Atlantic one.

trigger_context: Compare the evidence behind the 1713 Asiento and its 1750 termination.
raw_content:
They're closer in nominal tier than in actual evidential state, and the gap runs the opposite way from what you'd expect given that both rest on a read treaty.

**1713 is the best-evidenced node in Window 3.** [w3-1713-legal] and its four companion entries rest on the Assiento contract itself, live_verified, and the audit quotes it at article level: Article I for the thirty-year term and the 144,000 piezas at 4,800 a year, Article II for the single composite duty of 33⅓ per pieza. [w3-1713-sovereign] pulls the Spanish crown's fourth part of the gain plus five per cent of England's three parts off the same instrument, and [w3-1713-records] cites Article XXXIX for the conveyance of six named predecessor asentistas. When an entry can tell you which article a number came from, you are looking at someone who opened the document. The only thing keeping those warrants Open is Sperling sitting unread beside the primary.

**1750 has a read treaty and a claim the treaty cannot carry.** [w3-1750-financial] cites the Treaty of Madrid text, live_verified on archive.org, alongside Palmer's *Human Cargoes* at citation_only. The termination and the £100,000 payment are the sort of thing a treaty text settles. But the entry's second sentence does the real work: it argues that the licence is relinquished while the classification franchise survives, and that "Asiento-classified voyages continue for another five-plus decades post-1750." A termination treaty cannot establish what happened after termination. That is a carriage-volume claim, and the only source in this corpus that could test it is the Voyages Database behind [w3-1725-financial] — which is live_verified, but which the 1750 entry does not cite.

So the asymmetry is not about source quality. Both entries rest on read primaries. It is that 1713's claims stay inside the document and 1750's step outside it, into the survival argument, without picking up a source on the way.

That matters more than it might, because the survival claim is not incidental — it is the corpus's own N1 Collapse-Survival pattern, and 1750 is one of its two anchor instances. The other is [w3-1720-financial], which argues the Bubble Act armoured the classification before the crash, and which rests on a Wikipedia page and a tier C internal file. The pattern's strongest statement, [w3-1725-financial], is separately well sourced on the Voyages Database. My reading, and this is me joining entries the corpus keeps apart: the N1 pattern has one properly evidenced leg, 1725, and two weaker ones that both make the same unsourced move of asserting continuity past a documented rupture.

One thing worth adding about what the 1713 material lets you see, because it is the same operation appearing twice. [w3-1701-sovereign] records the French and Spanish crowns each taking a quarter shareholding in the asiento company at 100,000 livres apiece — sovereigns holding capital in the operating company rather than licensing it from outside. Twelve years later [w3-1713-sovereign] has the Spanish crown taking a fourth part of the gain plus a cut of England's share. Same structure, different licence holder, and the 1713 contract's Article XXXIX explicitly conveys the predecessors' concessions forward. That is the franchise persisting across operators, shown at article level in a read primary — which is exactly the claim the 1750 entry wants to make about the period after termination and cannot yet support. Note also that the 1701 and 1662 entries [w3-1662-corporate] are tier B on a single reference-work page, so the upstream chain is thinner than the 1713 node it feeds.

triage.summary: The 1750 entry's claim that Asiento-classified voyages continued post-termination rests on the Treaty of Madrid but lacks the carriage-volume evidence from the Voyages Database that could test it; this same unsourced continuity move appears in w3-1720-financial, leaving the N1 Collapse-Survival pattern with only w3-1725-financial properly evidenced.
triage.note: The 1713 material shows franchise persistence across operators at article level (Article XXXIX), which is the exact structural move 1750 wants to make about post-termination but cannot yet support from sources. w3-1701-sovereign and w3-1662-corporate form a thin upstream chain (tier B, single reference work) feeding into 1713. The asymmetry is not source quality but that 1713 stays inside its document while both 1750 and 1720 step outside it into survival claims without picking up sources. Operator should audit whether the Voyages Database citation belongs in w3-1750-financial and whether the N1 pattern's evidential architecture needs revision given this gap.

trigger_context: Are there entries with no sources at all?
raw_content:
Yes, a handful, and they fall into three quite different categories worth keeping apart.

**Deliberate absence, declared.** [E-W0-010-01] is the clean case: the star fort / mound grid on a silicon substrate. The entry states outright that its framings have no scholarly support, notes that "star fort" is a 16th-century bastioned-artillery form anachronistic to 1100, and says no source is attached rather than manufacture a citation. It signs off "Empty beats fabricated." That is not a gap; it is the audit refusing to launder a claim, and it is the most creditable thing in this category. [E-W0-006-01] does something similar without going all the way to zero sources — it carries a source but declares itself HELD-NULL because that source says the Mali ships never returned.

**Structural absence, undeclared.** [w3-1711-financial] is the significant one. The South Sea Company's incorporation, its receipt of the Asiento, and the debt-for-stock conversion — no source line at all. This is not a peripheral entry: the framework spine says Track A installs via the SSC 1713 renewal, the insurance-actuarial construct names it, and the W6 dossier on the 2023 bank failures [E-W6-041-01] treats it as the pattern's origin. The entry itself says it exists because those two things pointed at it and could not resolve it. So it is a placeholder created by the graph, honestly labelled as such, but nothing has been put under it.

The 1967 Utah Memorial entries, [E-W6-016-01] and [E-W6-016-02], are the same shape and more exposed. The claim is that a state legislature formally challenged the 14th Amendment's ratification and Congress never responded — and the entry's own argument is that if this holds, several later layers collapse. A claim structured as load-bearing, carrying nothing. Similarly [E-W6-029-04], "The Silicon Altar," which is the corpus's closing statement, and [E-W6-029-05], its five structural constraints. Peroration is where sourcing usually thins, but these are stated as findings.

**Interpretive coda.** [E-W4-008-01] on taxonomy entering the vernacular through Latin-to-German translation, and several of the W6 military sync entries — [E-W6-007-02], [E-W6-007-06], [E-W6-007-07], [E-W6-015-02] on the civil-rights narrative, [E-W6-019-04] on the tough-on-crime framing. These are mostly framing sentences attached to sourced neighbours, and the cost of their being unsourced is lower.

Two observations across the set. First, the W3 and W5 windows almost never do this — W5's method is a sourced newspaper page per assertion, and where it can't get one the entry says "Asserted (window content, unsourced)" in the assessment line and marks the warrant Open. That is the corpus policing itself. W6 does it much less consistently, which is where most of the undeclared absences sit.

Second, and this is my reading rather than the corpus's: the unsourced entries cluster at the two ends of the argument, the deep-time substrate and the present-day conclusion, and thin out in the middle where the instruments are. That is the normal shape of an argument built outward from documents — the documented centre holds and the interpretive ends float. It's worth knowing that the parts of this corpus that read as most decisive are, on average, the parts with least under them.

triage.summary: The corpus contains clusters of unsourced entries in three categories: deliberate undeclared absence (mainly W6), structural placeholders created by the graph (SSC 1713, Utah Memorial, Silicon Altar), and interpretive codas (framing sentences). W3 and W5 police this inconsistently; W6 does not. Unsourced entries concentrate at argument endpoints (substrate and conclusion) rather than the documented middle, meaning the most decisive-reading sections carry the least sourcing.
triage.note: This is a diagnosis of method rather than a single correction. The answer flags that W6 lacks the audit discipline present in W3/W5 (which mark unsourced assertions explicitly). The observation about argument shape — sourced centre, interpretive float at the ends — is a structural pattern worth recording: it means confidence should track proximity to documents, and the peroration and foundation are doing interpretive work without equal evidentiary footing. Two entries are flagged as load-bearing but unsourced: [w3-1711-financial] (SSC incorporation and Asiento) and [E-W6-016-01]/[E-W6-016-02] (Utah Memorial ratification challenge). These are candidates for staged sourcing or explicit placeholder marking.

trigger_context: How solid is the corpus on Reconstruction-era violence?
raw_content:
Better than most of Window 5, and for a specific reason: the Reconstruction violence entries are the place where the corpus has federal investigative primaries available and uses them.

The strong core is the congressional-investigation set. Eutaw 1870 [E-W5-015-01] and Meridian 1871 [E-W5-016-01] rest on the KKK hearings testimony from Alabama and Mississippi, both live_verified on archive.org. Clinton 1875 [E-W5-020-01] rests on the Boutwell report on Mississippi. These are tier A and read, and they are the right kind of source — sworn testimony taken close to the events by a body with subpoena power. Opelousas 1868 [E-W5-013-01] and Coushatta 1874 [E-W5-019-02] are on contemporary newspaper pages rather than investigations, also read. Fort Pillow [E-W5-010-01] has the 1864 congressional report itself, which is why that entry can say flatly that a federal investigation later contradicted the initial press account.

The legal spine underneath is equally solid. Cruikshank [E-W5-021-02] is tier A on the Cornell text, and it is the ruling that made the federal remedy for Colfax unavailable — so the corpus has the massacre and the holding that followed it, both sourced.

Where it thins is in a way that is easy to mistake for weakness but is really a change of object. Memphis 1866 [E-W5-012-05], Hamburg 1876 [E-W5-021-04], Thibodaux 1887 [E-W5-027-05], Ocoee 1920 [E-W5-053-03], Springfield 1908 [E-W5-043-02] — these are tier C and their sources are Chronicling America *search queries*, not particular pages. A search URL measures how much coverage a term generated. That is a real and checkable thing, and it is what the information lane is actually about; but it is not evidence about the massacre, and an entry resting on it should not be read as documenting the event. Memphis is the sharpest case, because the violence entry and the framing entry cite the same search.

What raises my confidence in the whole set is that the corpus catches its own failures here twice. At [E-W5-010-02] the Sand Creek framing entry says the Denver claim is untested, that the paper actually sourced reported Sand Creek *as an atrocity*, and that the corpus appears to hold no Denver papers for the period — so the claim cannot be checked from what is held. At [E-W5-019-04] the Freedman's Bank entry says the sourced page is from two months *before* the collapse and is deferential to Douglass, so the blame claim is not established at that date and needs later pages. Those are two places where the audit measured its own hypothesis and reported that the measurement went against it. That is unusual, and it makes me trust the surrounding coverage-differential claims more than I otherwise would — though note that neither entry has been *revised*, only annotated.

One structural caution. The bucket assessments are candid about coverage: Memphis's year is "4 of 5 sourced" with one unsourced, 1871 is "1 of 5 entries sourced," 1875 is "1 of 3." So the individual violence entries are frequently well sourced while the years around them are half-empty. The corpus is stronger on the massacres than on the context it places them in — which is roughly the opposite of the pattern in Window 0, where the framework is confident and the instruments unread.

trigger_context: Give me a claim I could go verify myself right now.
raw_content:
The Bubble Act chronology at [w3-1720-financial].

The entry claims the Bubble Act received Royal Assent in June 1720, three months *before* the South Sea crash of September–December, and that this inverts the standard reading of the Act as post-crash regulation. It further claims the Act legally cemented the SSC monopoly by criminalising competing joint-stock formations — armour installed *before* the failure, not remedy after it.

This is the best candidate for four reasons. It is falsifiable in a single afternoon: statute dates are in the Statutes of the Realm, and the assent date either precedes the crash or it doesn't. It rests on the corpus's weakest sourcing for a claim of its size — a Wikipedia page on the statute plus an internal timeline file at tier C, with no monograph and no primary text read. The corpus itself flags that it is arguing against the standard account, so you know exactly what you are testing against. And it is load-bearing: [w3-1720-corporate] builds the SSC-as-sole-Track-A-operator claim on it, and it is one of the two anchor instances of the Collapse-Survival N1 pattern, the other being [w3-1725-financial].

Two things to check rather than one, because they can come apart. The date is probably fine — I'd expect June 1720 to hold, and the "passed before the bubble burst" point is not actually controversial among historians of the period. What is genuinely contestable is the *causal* reading. The standard account has the Act promoted by the South Sea Company itself to suppress rival subscription schemes competing for investor money, which is close to the corpus's claim but arrives by a different route: company self-interest during the mania, rather than the state pre-emptively armouring a classification franchise. And there's a well-known argument that enforcement of the Act against rival companies in August helped *trigger* the collapse rather than survive it. If that holds, the entry's framing — armour that let the classification outlive the bond — needs adjusting even though its chronology stands.

So the verification has a real chance of splitting: date confirmed, interpretation complicated. That is more useful than a clean pass.

If you want a second, [w3-1725-financial] is checkable directly — the Voyages Database is live and queryable, and the claim is that British Atlantic voyages under Asiento licence peak in the 1724–28 window, five years after the crash. That one is already sourced to the database, so you would be confirming rather than filling a hole, but it is the empirical leg the whole N1 pattern stands on and it would be worth knowing whether the peak is really there.

triage.summary: The Bubble Act's June 1720 Royal Assent date and its causal role in securing the South Sea Company's monopoly by criminalising rival joint-stock formations are testable against primary statute records and secondary historiography; the chronology is likely sound but the causal framing (state pre-emptive armouring vs. company self-interest during mania) is genuinely contested and may require interpretation adjustment even if dates hold.
triage.note: Two-part verification: (1) Assent date in Statutes of the Realm — probably firm, not controversial. (2) Causal reading — historians debate whether the Act was promoted by SSC self-interest during the mania or represented state pre-emptive monopoly protection, and whether enforcement in August 1720 *triggered* rather than survived the collapse. Sourcing for the entry is weak (Wikipedia + tier C timeline, no monograph or primary text). Load-bearing claim: [w3-1720-corporate] and both instances of Collapse-Survival N1 pattern depend on it. Secondary candidate: [w3-1725-financial] voyages peak 1724–28, already sourced to Voyages Database and queryable; confirms empirical leg of N1 pattern.

trigger_context: Has anyone actually read the sources behind the Meridian massacre entry?
raw_content:
Yes. [E-W5-016-01] cites the Mississippi volume of the 1872 KKK hearings — the "insurrectionstate11goverich" scan on archive.org — and it is marked live_verified, meaning someone doing this audit opened it and recorded what it says. Same for the Alabama volume behind Eutaw [E-W5-015-01]. These are tier A congressional testimony, and they are among the genuinely read sources in Window 5 rather than the citation_only monographs that pad out Window 0.

But I want to be precise about what "read" gets you here, because there is a gap between the source's state and the entry's state.

The Meridian entry has *no body*. The title is the whole claim. Its assessment line reads "Proven (1 of 5 entries sourced, tier B) · Asserted (4 unsourced)" with warrant Open — and that assessment describes the 1871 bucket as a whole, not the massacre entry specifically. So the entry is a sourced pointer: a verified primary attached to a title, with the detail either living in a dossier or not yet extracted. You can follow the citation to real testimony. What you cannot do is read this corpus and learn what the testimony says about Meridian — the number killed, the sequence, who testified, what the committee concluded. None of that has been brought across.

Compare Fort Pillow [E-W5-010-01], which has the same shape, and then compare both to the entries where the audit clearly worked the source: [E-W5-019-04] reports that the Freedman's Bank page it opened is dated two months before the collapse and is deferential to Douglass, which contradicts the entry's own framing. That is what it looks like when someone reads a source and lets it push back. Meridian has no such friction, which tells me the volume was located and confirmed rather than mined.

So the honest answer is that the *evidence* behind Meridian is strong and opened, and the *entry* is thin — and those two facts point in opposite directions when you ask "how solid is this." The tier is doing more work than the prose. If you wanted to strengthen anything in the Reconstruction cluster at low cost, this is it: the testimony is already open on the shelf.

triage.summary: Meridian massacre entry is sourced to tier A testimony but contains no extractive prose—it is a verified pointer without detail work. Fort Pillow and the Freedman's Bank entry show the contrast between citation confirmation and actual source mining, revealing a gap between evidence strength and entry depth that affects how the tier rating should be read.
triage.note: The answer identifies a systematic problem in Window 5: entries may pass verification (source located and opened) without undergoing the interpretive friction that real reading produces. Meridian's assessment tier describes the 1871 bucket, not the entry itself, masking this thinness. Low-cost remediation opportunity: the KKK testimony volume is already open and could be mined for detail. This points to a possible audit-process gap worth examining across the cluster.
